questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: State the thesis an observing log commits to and the claim it defends
questions.stem: Tomas argues in his notebook that poor seeing ruined his photometry of a faint nebula; state the thesis his paragraph commits to.

answer.exemplar: Tomas's thesis is that poor atmospheric seeing, not faulty equipment or his own technique, caused the blurred photometry of the faint nebula, and that recording seeing conditions alongside each image is therefore the reliable way to judge his results.

questions.explanation: A thesis states the writer's position and can be defended. Tomas blames seeing conditions rather than equipment, and the exemplar keeps that single claim without drifting into how he felt about the night.
questions.hint: Look for the single claim the writer defends.

answer.exemplar: Quoting the mentor's exact phrase lets Sasha appeal to a named authority and preserve the compactness of the original advice, so the reader receives the expert's judgement in the mentor's own wording instead of Sasha's paraphrase.

questions.explanation: Quotation lends the argument borrowed authority and keeps the source's precision. Paraphrase blurs who said what, and quotation without attribution would lose the standing that makes it persuasive.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a closing question organises the observations above it
questions.stem: A log paragraph on comet tails ends by asking whether dust or ice drives the glow; explain what that question does for the paragraph.

answer.exemplar: Ending the paragraph on a question makes the earlier observations read as evidence gathered towards that question rather than as a list of sightings, so the paragraph gains direction and points the reader towards the writer's next line of enquiry.

questions.explanation: A closing question converts prior details into evidence for an unresolved issue, giving the paragraph direction. Ending on a flat statement or an unrelated aside would leave the observations without an organising purpose.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how quoting another observer's phrase lends weight to a judgement
questions.stem: Elif quotes an older observer's phrase about steady hands and poor patience; explain how the quotation strengthens her judgement.

answer.exemplar: The quotation strengthens Elif's judgement because the older observer's phrasing carries an authority the log cannot claim for itself, and by quoting rather than paraphrasing she lets the reader hear the criticism in the voice of someone who has earned the right to make it.

questions.explanation: Quoting an older observer borrows standing and keeps the wording that made the remark memorable, so the judgement lands harder. Paraphrase reduces it to the writer's opinion and loses that authority.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Compare two different endings and the expectations each one creates
questions.stem: Compare two endings to a log entry about the Milky Way and explain what each one makes the reader expect.

answer.exemplar: One ending, on the observer's drive home under the same arch of stars, makes the reader expect a private continuation, while the ending on a dated sketch makes the reader expect the entry to belong to a longer series, and the contrast shows how the last sentence sets the horizon of what follows.

questions.explanation: Different endings set different expectations, since the drive home promises something personal while a dated record promises continuation in the series. The ending controls how the entry is read backwards.
questions.hint: Ask what each ending promises the reader next.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a revision makes possible for the argument of an entry
questions.stem: Compare a first draft and a revised draft of the same observing log entry and explain what the revision makes possible.

answer.exemplar: The revision makes possible an argument the first draft could not carry, because once the repeated impressions of the seeing are compressed into a single judgement, the writer has space to set that judgement against the club's chart and reach a conclusion a reader can check.

questions.explanation: Revising for length is revising for argument, since space freed by cutting repetition can be spent on the comparison that produces a conclusion. A revision that only trims words makes the entry shorter, not stronger.
questions.hint: Ask what the freed space is now used for.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an imperative ending sets the reader's expectations

answer.exemplar: The imperative ending turns the entry from a closed record into an open one, because a promise of a future check implies that the present observation is provisional and that the log will continue, so the reader expects the question to be revisited rather than settled.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how revision should settle a self-contradiction in a record
questions.stem: Cleo's entry contradicts itself about cloud cover; explain how revision should resolve the inconsistency.

answer.exemplar: Revision should settle the contradiction rather than hide it, so the writer checks which note matches the observing record, corrects the mistaken sentence, and briefly notes the correction so that later readers of the log can trust the remaining observations.

answer.exemplar: The thesis would claim that a carefully aligned home-built instrument lets a determined beginner reach the faint targets that matter, which is a position the entry can support with records of successful observation and which a reader can test against their own equipment.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why dividing an entry into neat paragraphs does not create unity
questions.stem: Zoe's log entry contains four topics in four paragraphs; explain what has gone wrong with its unity.

answer.exemplar: Unity is not a matter of paragraph boundaries, so splitting the entry into four clean paragraphs does not by itself make it whole; what the entry needs is a single controlling idea, perhaps a season of observations, against which each separate topic can be read as part of one continuing enquiry.

questions.explanation: Dividing material into separate paragraphs separates it but does not connect it, so the reader meets four topics with no reason to hold them together. Unity comes from a controlling idea the paragraphs share.
questions.hint: Separate is not the same as joined.
